central_model: Views and Beyond (V&B): select stakeholder-relevant views, document each with a standard view packet, then add cross-view documentation that maps and integrates them; align views with IEEE 1471 stakeholder–concern–viewpoint–view concepts.

architecture_principles.principle: Use multiple purpose-specific views rather than one universal representation.
architecture_principles.why_it_manages_complexity: Each view restricts attention to one structure while the overall package preserves the system’s multiple simultaneous structures.

architecture_principles.principle: Select views from explicit stakeholder needs and concerns, then prioritize the minimum useful set.
architecture_principles.why_it_manages_complexity: A stakeholder/view table prevents collecting detail that serves no review question and makes trade-offs visible.

architecture_principles.principle: Use a defined vocabulary/style for every view, including element types, relationship types, constraints, notation, and analysis methods.
architecture_principles.why_it_manages_complexity: Typed elements and relations prevent category drift—for example, treating a contrast, causal link, and validation result as interchangeable.

architecture_principles.principle: Make each view packet self-explanatory through a primary representation, element catalog, context, variability, and rationale.
architecture_principles.why_it_manages_complexity: The representation stays readable while definitions, exceptions, and reasons remain attached to the relevant view.

architecture_principles.principle: Treat cross-view mappings and cross-view rationale as first-class documentation.
architecture_principles.source_locator: §2.5 “Mapping between views” and “Cross-view rationale,” pp.6–8; Figure 2
architecture_principles.why_it_manages_complexity: Mappings preserve traceability across representations and expose whether separately extracted facts form one coherent account.

architecture_principles.principle: Record consistency and known inconsistencies among views.
architecture_principles.why_it_manages_complexity: Conflicts can be retained as explicit evidence states instead of being silently reconciled or lost.

unit_and_boundary_rules: Treat the report as the top-level documentation package, not as the study itself; one report may describe multiple studies, analyses, or validation activities.

Represent a study as the bounded empirical context: cohort/sample, design, timepoint(s), and analysis setting. Its external context should state population, measurement environment, and stated constraints. Basis: §2.5 context diagram, p.5; §4.1 environment, p.12.

Represent the causal workflow as a view of ordered analytic/runtime-like activity; represent causal links as typed relations in an element catalog, not merely prose claims. Basis: §2.2 distinguishes interacting elements from code units, p.3; §2.5 element catalog, p.5.

Represent each contrast separately from a causal link: a contrast specifies the compared conditions/groups/exposures; a link specifies the asserted directed causal relation and its assumptions. Connect them in a mapping rather than collapsing them into one record.
Represent validation as a distinct element/activity with a declared target, method, result, and scope; map it to the link, workflow step, or contrast it supports, challenges, or reproduces.
Maintain source evidence as a separate provenance view: locate each extracted assertion in the supplied report and map evidence items to study, workflow, link, contrast, and validation elements.
Use combined views only when there is a strong correspondence between their elements; otherwise retain separate views and create explicit mappings. Basis: §2.4 Step 2, p.5.
provenance_and_evidence_rules: Give every extracted element a stable identifier and a source locator; use the directory concept to index elements, relations, properties, and where they are defined and used. Basis: §2.5 “Directory,” p.7.
For each causal assertion, retain its view-specific representation plus its evidence link; do not let an evidence citation substitute for defining the asserted relation.

Document the rationale for analytic/causal choices and, where reported, alternatives considered; distinguish this rationale from evidence that the claim is true. Basis: §3 requirement 12, p.11; §2.5 rationale, pp.5, 7.
Capture configuration/identification metadata for each report and extracted representation, including status/version or revision where available. Basis: §3 requirements 1 and 10, p.10.
Record unresolved discrepancies explicitly as known cross-view inconsistencies, with their scope and affected identifiers. Basis: §3 requirement 11, p.11.
Use a glossary for causal and omics-specific terms whose meaning is study-specific or otherwise ambiguous. Basis: §2.5 glossary, p.7; §3 requirement 1, p.10.

adaptations_for_causal_multiomics_review.proposed_component: Review documentation roadmap plus stakeholder/concern matrix
adaptations_for_causal_multiomics_review.use_in_review: Declare the review users and the questions each view answers—for example, which studies make a link, under what contrast, through which workflow, and with what validation/evidence.

adaptations_for_causal_multiomics_review.proposed_component: Six linked views: report, study-context, causal-workflow, causal-link, contrast, and validation/provenance
adaptations_for_causal_multiomics_review.use_in_review: Keep distinct structures legible while allowing each to use its own typed elements and relations.
For each link, define exposure, outcome, direction, omics layer(s), estimand/claim wording, assumptions or adjustment strategy if reported, linked contrast, and linked evidence.

adaptations_for_causal_multiomics_review.proposed_component: Context diagram per study or workflow
adaptations_for_causal_multiomics_review.use_in_review: Bound what belongs to the analyzed study from external cohort, assay, reference resource, or validation environment.
Map report → study → workflow → link → contrast → validation → source-evidence, supporting one-to-many relations without flattening them.
State which review fields legitimately vary across designs, omics modalities, causal estimators, and validation types, versus which identifiers and provenance fields remain mandatory.

cautions: This source supplies an architecture-documentation framework, not causal-inference criteria; it does not determine whether a reported causal link is valid.
Do not impose a fixed view set mechanically: V&B recommends views useful for the stakeholders and system at hand. (§2.1, p.3; §4.3, p.14)
A mapping between views supports integration but does not itself prove consistency; preserve and report known inconsistencies. (§3, p.11)

V&B’s correspondence heuristic supports combining views only when their elements strongly correspond; causal link, contrast, validation, and evidence should remain distinct unless that condition is met. (§2.4 Step 2, p.5)
